chapter: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
title: Segregated seating played for comedy in the Nazarro act
summary: Green explains the bit where Buck and Bubbles ask to sit downstairs while upstairs was for blacks; the interviewer asks if it parodied blacks and Green says it was authentic.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: So here was this white family that had an act. And they introduced these blacks in their act to add the comedy.
Yeah.
And the blacks would play what sort of -- what role? How would you describe their role?
Well, that was it. They were like children, you see, youngsters, you know, and it was based on this thing about -- like whites downstairs and the other, blacks

upstairs, you see. And that's how they'd be chasing each other. They'd come -- like in downstairs in the theater, see, but it wasn't allowed, see. But they're creating this argument by saying, "Hey mister, Let's -- can't I sit over here? Can't I?"

And then Buck be telling, he said, "Why, no. You -- we ain't supposed to be down here. We supposed to be up yonder in the buzzard's roof, you know. And he looked right at him when he said buzzard, see, because the buzzard's a real black bird, man. He's black as you can get, you know. understand"
(Laughter)

So he says, "Oh, no. We paid, show fare's paid. I tell you what. We go up there and ask that man, and we pointed at that man, and the man is in the process of balancing five people, man, you know, up over his shoulders, and he's holding -- Don't be hollering you understand "(unintelligible)" holler at me. And they "You can't hit me started "(unintelligible)" because you can't pick up that nothing in here to throw. "(inaudible), you know, and he'd run up on the stage, you know, and he started to running between Nat Nazarra's legs, you understand.

And just like goosing somebody, you know, and he -- he don't want to drop his sons, and Buck run through here and stand -- he'd have to stoop down to run through there. But each time it's like a goose. You understand? And you run through -- he's running around, come through here, and it go right through there, you know. And it's like a goose. "Hey,
don't drop me.
(Laughter and unintelligible conversation)
So the sons get in/on it, you know. "Oh, (unintelligible) yeah, I ain't got up there yet, you know." And say, -- that's what happened, see.

So they were in a sense almost parodying the fact that there was an area in the audience for the blacks and an area for the whites, and they came as if they were just walking into the theater foolishly.
(Laughter)
Was it also a parody on the blacks, you think, in any way? Without really knowing -- Of, you know, really --

Well, that was actually authentic at that time. You know, that was -- they did -- some theaters did have that. They would have like whites downstairs, blacks upstairs. Understand? So (inaudible) they guess it was -- I don't know whose idea it was to have this, you know.

See, Mr. Buck, he had raise the legs, you know, and he wore these pants up, you know, like they was almost like knickers, you see. And he wore a cap, you know, and like a sweater like this here, and he go running -- he'd come in and he'd create this -- in the midst of a great stunt, you know, because, I mean, (inaudible) this man, one man, how the heck can he hold up five people, you know, or something, and it was -- well, the kinds sons, they could do all types of acrobatics and things, you
know. And one of them get onstage and lay down, put his hand out. That was the -- that's a beautiful stunt.
Terrific idea.
Yeah, he was a great show --
Terrific comedy.
He's about one of the greatest we had, showmen, he knowed all the ins and outs about entertainment, Nat Nazarra, see. Yeah.
